title: Best sun hats 2026: certified UPF vs. style-only straw
description: Best sun hats 2026: certified UPF vs. style-only straw. Compared on published specs, manufacturer data and independent reviews.
lede: The $270 Helen Kaminski has the better craftsmanship. The $52 Madewell is the one with a published UPF claim behind it. Craft and certified sun protection do not arrive in the same hat here.

sections.heading: How we compared
paragraphs: Packability and shape retention are what separate these hats, and both show up clearly in owner reviews: how far a hat can be crushed into a bag, and how much reshaping it needs once it comes out.
A floppy brim that blows into your face is a real usability problem that photo reviews never capture.

sections.heading: Lack of Color Wave Hat — the Instagram hat
paragraphs: The Wave is everywhere on Pinterest and Instagram, and the reason is simple: it photographs exceptionally well. The natural straw curves in a photogenic drape that looks expensive. The 10cm brim is wide enough for casual sun protection without overwhelming the face.

Packability is the Wave's surprise feature — the straw returns to shape after crushing better than any other straw hat in this group, and owners report it needing only light hand-shaping after repeated packing. The trade-off is that Lack of Color publishes no UPF rating for it at all, and an open straw weave is the weakest sun protection in this group. If actual sun protection is your priority, the Wave is not your hat.
At $89, it is the second most expensive non-luxury pick. You're paying primarily for the aesthetic and the brand's social media presence, both of which are real if intangible value.

sections.heading: Helen Kaminski Provence 12 — the heirloom
paragraphs: The Provence 12 is handwoven fine raffia with a 12cm brim — the widest in this comparison and the most structurally rigid. On the head it feels like quality: the hat doesn't shift in moderate wind and the inner band is adjustable with a small drawstring. This is the hat you buy once and keep for 10 years.

At $270, the justification is craftsmanship and durability, not UPF performance. Helen Kaminski publishes no UPF rating for the Provence 12, and a woven raffia brim leaves gaps that a certified UPF 50+ fabric does not — the $72 Solbari has the test certificates this hat does not. If you're buying the Helen Kaminski for sun protection, there are better options at a third of the price.

Packability is limited — the rigid raffia structure does not compress well without risking permanent creases. This is a destination hat you wear at the villa, not a travel hat you stuff into overhead bins.

sections.heading: Madewell Packable Straw Hat — best value
paragraphs: The Madewell is one of only two hats here that carries a UPF claim at all — UPF 40+, which corresponds to roughly 97.5% of UV blocked through the fabric — and it costs $52. The cinch strap on the inside lets you tighten the fit and also holds it in a collapsed tube shape for packing. Owners report it coming out of a packed bag ready to wear without reshaping.

The 8cm brim is the narrowest here and offers less face coverage than the 10-12cm options. On sunny days with high UV index, the narrower brim means more coverage with sunscreen. The hat is a practical travel companion, not a statement piece — but that understated positioning is exactly right for a $52 purchase.
Madewell's quality control on this hat has been inconsistent across production runs. Worth checking on arrival.

sections.heading: Solbari Packable UPF 50+ — best sun protection
paragraphs: Solbari is an Australian brand focused entirely on UV protection — not fashion, not lifestyle branding. The Packable UPF 50+ hat is the only hat here that states a UPF 50+ rating from the brand. The 10cm brim includes a chin strap for high-wind conditions.

The hat compresses into a flat disk and springs back to shape reliably. The fabric feels lighter and more technical than the natural straw options, which is a style trade-off — it doesn't have the resort aesthetic of the Lack of Color or Helen Kaminski. At $72, it is the practical choice for beach activities, hiking, or travel where you need verified UV coverage rather than a great photo.
The chin strap is a feature that most fashion-hat buyers overlook and then desperately wish they had on the first windy day. With the Solbari, it's removable if you don't need it.

faqs.q: Does a higher brim width actually protect more of your face?
faqs.a: Yes, but the geometry matters. A 10cm brim shades the face at a sun angle of roughly 40° from horizontal — so if the sun is lower in the sky (morning, late afternoon, or winter), you get full face coverage. At high noon with the sun directly overhead, even a 12cm brim leaves the lower face exposed. For maximum coverage, combine a wide brim with SPF on the lower face and neck.

faqs.q: Is UPF 40+ the same as SPF 40?
faqs.a: No — UPF and SPF measure different things. UPF (Ultraviolet Protection Factor) is for fabrics and measures both UV-A and UV-B block through the material. SPF is for sunscreen and measures UV-B burn protection on skin. A UPF 40 hat blocks roughly 97.5% of UV-B through the fabric; SPF 40 sunscreen provides similar UV-B protection when properly applied to exposed skin.

faqs.q: Will a straw hat last if I wear it in rain?
faqs.a: Natural straw hats, including the Lack of Color Wave and the Helen Kaminski, can warp if soaked and then dried in the wrong shape. Light rain is usually fine. Heavy rain or submersion will distort the brim. The Solbari and Madewell's synthetic-blend materials are more water-tolerant — they won't warp if caught in a downpour.

faqs.q: How does the Lack of Color Wave Hat pack in a carry-on?
faqs.a: Better than you'd expect for natural straw. The brim has a slight memory-foam quality — it bounces back from compression. Owners report it comes out of a packed bag needing only light hand-shaping. It does not roll into a tube like the Madewell or Solbari — it needs its own dedicated space or a hat box for overhead bin storage.

faqs.q: Which hat is best for a face with a high forehead?
faqs.a: The Helen Kaminski Provence 12 with its 12cm brim provides the most face coverage and suits prominent foreheads well. The structured brim also means it doesn't tilt forward the way floppy straws do. The Solbari's 10cm brim is a close second, with the benefit of a chin strap to keep the fit stable.

faqs.q: How do I know if my straw hat has real UPF or just a label?
faqs.a: The only reliable method is third-party testing. Solbari publishes its test certificates (AATCC TM183 or equivalent). Madewell's UPF 40+ claim is backed by fabric certification. The Lack of Color Wave doesn't make a UPF claim — which at least is honest, since straw of this weave blocks well short of the 98% a UPF 50+ certification implies. Be skeptical of any fashion hat that adds 'UPF 50+' to the marketing copy without a test certificate.

faqs.q: Can I wear these hats in the pool?
faqs.a: The natural straw hats (Lack of Color, Helen Kaminski, Madewell) should not be submerged — they will deform. The Solbari and Brixton Joanna are more water-tolerant but still aren't designed for swimming. None of these are swim hats. For poolside UV protection, keep them on the lounge chair, not on your head in the water.

offerNotes.lack-of-color-wave-hat: Best aesthetics — the most photogenic hat here, packs surprisingly well, but no published UPF rating and the weakest sun protection here.
offerNotes.brixton-joanna-hat: Best boho/western style — packable brim and adjustable band at a mid-range price.
offerNotes.helen-kaminski-hat: Best for longevity — handwoven raffia you'll wear for 10 years, but UV protection doesn't justify the premium.
offerNotes.madewell-packable-straw-hat: Best value — certified UPF 40+ at $52, cinch strap, packs into a tube for travel.
offerNotes.solbari-packable-sun-hat: Best UV protection — the only hat here with a certified UPF 50+ rating, with a chin strap.

pinDescription: Only one of these hats carries a certified UPF 50+ rating — and it is not the $270 luxury straw. UPF claims vs. what the brands actually publish.
methodology: This comparison is desk research. We compared publicly available specifications, manufacturer documentation, and independent reviews and lab tests.

products.review: The Wave is everywhere on Pinterest because it genuinely photographs well — the natural straw drape looks expensive. Packability is better than expected for straw, bouncing back after compression. Lack of Color publishes no UPF rating for it, and an open straw weave is the weakest sun protection here, so if that is the priority, look elsewhere.
pros: Handcrafted natural straw with photogenic drape
Recovers from compression better than other straw hats
Extensive color and trim variations available
cons: No published UPF rating — weakest sun protection here

products.review: The Joanna's packable brim and adjustable inner band make it a practical companion with a western/boho aesthetic. Brixton publishes no UPF rating either, so it sits with the Lack of Color and Helen Kaminski as a style-first hat. The $65 price sits in the middle of the group with reasonable value for the quality.
pros: Adjustable inner band fits most head sizes
Packable brim with better shape recovery than natural straw
Western aesthetic works for multiple outfit styles
cons: No published UPF rating — coverage varies by color and weave

products.review: Handwoven fine raffia, a 12cm brim, and a build quality that will last a decade — the Provence 12 is the only hat here worth passing down. Helen Kaminski publishes no UPF rating for it, and the $270 price cannot be justified by sun protection alone. Buy it if you want an heirloom beach hat, not if you want maximum UV defense.
pros: Handwoven raffia with premium finish and feel
cons: Does not pack into a bag without risk of permanent creases

products.review: At $52, the Madewell is one of only two hats here with a UPF claim behind it — UPF 40+, where the $270 Helen Kaminski has none. The cinch strap lets you collapse it into a tube for carry-on packing. The 8cm brim is the narrowest here and leaves more of the lower face exposed, so pair it with SPF on your nose and chin on high-UV days.
pros: Certified UPF 40+ — rare at this price
Cinch strap allows tube packing for carry-ons
cons: 8cm brim is narrowest — least lower-face coverage

products.review: Solbari builds hats for sun safety, not Instagram, and the published test certificates back it up. It is the only hat here rated UPF 50+, which corresponds to at least 98% of UV blocked through the fabric. Chin strap (removable), 10cm brim, and packs flat — it's the practical choice for beach days, travel, or any outdoor use where UV protection is non-negotiable.
pros: Certified UPF 50+ — the only hat here with test certificates
Removable chin strap for wind stability
cons: Technical aesthetic — less resort-glamour than straw options

recommendedFor.lack-of-color-wave-hat: Resort photography and Pinterest content where aesthetics matter more than certified UV protection.
recommendedFor.brixton-joanna-hat: Boho and western-style outfits where you want a packable hat with mid-range UV coverage.
recommendedFor.helen-kaminski-hat: Investment buyers who want a handwoven hat that will last 10+ years and don't mind packing carefully.
recommendedFor.madewell-packable-straw-hat: Travelers who want solid UV protection in a carry-on-friendly hat without spending more than $60.
recommendedFor.solbari-packable-sun-hat: Anyone who needs verified UPF 50+ protection — beach holidays, hiking, or post-surgery sun sensitivity.
